奚琴原為奚人弓弦樂器，唐末傳入中國，後傳至朝鮮半島與日本。韓國文獻無確切引入年代: The haegum began as a bowed instrument of the Xi people and reached China at the end of the Tang dynasty, then spread to the Korean peninsula and Japan. Korean sources give no exact date of introduction, but its name already appears in the Goryeo-period hanlimbyeolgok, so it can be assumed to have been played at least from then. In the Joseon dynasty the haegum was used in court sacrifice, processions, festivals and hyangak. The playing method also changed from the early practice of stopping the strings without bowing to bowing, and because there is no fingerboard it can produce more tone colours by pulling and releasing the string. From the 1960s there were improvements: in 1965 Park Hun-bong and Kim Bun-gi developed the low-pitched haegum, in 1967 Kim Gisu made the small haegum, and North Korean musicians developed a four-string small haegum and others.
奚琴在韓國傳統音樂中常見於宮廷與民間場合，亦見於朝鮮王朝時期的皇家祭祖儀式、遊行: In Korean traditional music the haegum is common in court and folk settings, and it appears in the Joseon dynasty royal ancestral rites, processions, festivals and hyangak. It is played by drawing a bow across two silk strings and can range from sorrowful to humorous. The modern improved four-string haegum is used in North Korea and in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture of China.
奚琴的發聲體為兩條絲弦，以木製弓摩擦發聲；琴身有棍狀頸與空心木質音箱。來源另稱其: The haegum's sounding bodies are two silk strings, set in vibration by a wooden bow; the body has a stick-like neck and a hollow wooden soundbox. The source also says that its making involves the eight materials metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, earth, hide and wood, hence the name eight sounds; the materials of the other parts are not stated, and no other materials are described.
奚琴音色溫潤而富有東方韻味，具有明暗兼具的音質特徵。其音域寬廣，可演奏高、中、低: The haegum's timbre is warm and has an Eastern character, with both light and dark qualities. Its range is wide: it can play in the high, middle and low registers, the high bright and clear, the middle mild and mellow, the low steady and strong. Because the soundbox is hollow wood, the resonance is full and deep, and the timbre has a moderate nasal quality, a distinctive weathered tone. Against the erhu it sounds slightly more archaic and bleak, with less brightness; against the morin khuur it is finer and softer. The sound wave from the friction of the bow echoes and resonates inside the wooden soundbox, so it can express both tender feeling and a bleak, far-reaching mood, with a strong local character and artistic pull.
奚琴（Haegum）是韓國傳統弓絃樂器，屬弦鳴樂器，由棍狀琴頸、空心木質音箱與兩: The haegum is a traditional Korean bowed string instrument, a chordophone made of a stick-like neck, a hollow wooden soundbox and two silk strings. The player holds it vertically on the knee and bows between the two strings, producing a continuous sound. It is used in court music and folk music, and also appears in Qing court sacrifice and in Manchu, Korean and Japanese traditional instruments. Because it is bowed and sounds continuously, some sources also class it among wind instruments.
用弓在弦上擦奏，透過弓毛與弦的摩擦力使弦震動。將樂器穩定持於身前。左手負責按弦或: The bow is drawn across the strings, and the friction of the hair on the string sets the string vibrating. Hold the instrument steadily in front of you. The left hand stops the strings, or changes the sounding length, to control the pitch, and the right hand sets the string vibrating. A chordophone sounds because the vibration of the string is amplified by the soundbox. Draw the bow evenly, using the weight of the arm rather than the strength of the wrist.
